title: Batched tokenizer latency and KV-cache design notes
content:
Purpose and context:
This note captures a concrete design and experiment plan for reducing tokenization-induced tail latency and for integrating a small but high-hit-rate tokenization KV cache into the serving runtime. It focuses on the runtime boundary between the text -> tokenizer stage and the rest of the inference pipeline (kernel selection, KV cache lookup, batch scheduling). Goal is to give clear tradeoffs and a minimal safe rollout path for a batched tokenizer + lightweight token cache that reduces per-request overhead without changing model semantics.

Problems we see today:
- Short requests (1–40 tokens) suffer from tokenizer overheads that are a large fraction of total SLO. Measured tokenization median ~2–6ms, 99th ~15–40ms (varies with concurrency and language).
- Tokenization is currently performed inline on request worker threads; this blocks scheduling decisions and complicates prefix caching and streaming.
- Repeated identical or near-identical inputs (bot probes, UI rerenders) cause repeated tokenization work despite being cacheable.
- Batched calls (many small requests arriving close together) are not currently amortizing tokenizer overhead.

Latency and cost targets:
- Tokenization tail target: P99 tokenization <= 10ms for 90% of traffic classes after optimizations for English-like inputs.
- For short inputs (<32 chars) aim for median tokenize <2ms when cache-hit or batched.
- End-to-end impact target: 15–40% reduction in median end-to-end latency for chat-like short requests; 5–20% reduction in P95 for mixed workloads.

Design overview (high level):
1) Fast tokenizer as a separate stage: extract tokenization into a dedicated, pluggable stage that runs on a tokenizer pool (CPU-optimized). The stage exposes both single-request and batch APIs and is integrated into request routing so scheduling is aware of tokenization completion.
2) Batched tokenizer: accumulate short incoming requests for a very small window (configurable 0–4ms) and feed them to a vectorized tokenizer worker that can reuse memory and thread-local state. Batch size heuristic: prefer batching requests that arrive within 2ms and are below 64 tokens.
3) Tokenization KV cache: lightweight LRU-like cache keyed by (raw_text, tokenizer_version, normalizer_hash, locale) -> token_ids + meta. Store small entries inline in process memory; evict aggressively per tenant. Provide shared in-memory (per-host) cache with optional global cache tier later.
4) Boundary contract: internal API returns a TokenizationEnvelope stringified form (token_ids, attention_mask_hint, bytes_consumed, tokenizer_version) so downstream runtime can decide kernel selection and KV cache interactions without re-tokenizing. The boundary remains language-agnostic: tokenizer implementation is a pluggable component.

Batching details and heuristics:
- Micro-batching window defaults to 2ms. If batch reaches N_max (e.g., 64 short requests) flush immediately.
- Requests carrying streaming/partial-input flags bypass batching to keep streaming latency low.
- Prioritize merging requests with similar normalization (e.g., same prefix) to increase cache hits within the batch.
- Backpressure: if tokenizer pool saturated, fallback to inline tokenization on request worker threads for high-priority traffic, or queue with timeout to avoid unbounded waits.

Tokenization KV cache semantics and implementation notes:
- Key composition: sha256(normalized_text || tokenizer_version || locale). Normalization includes unicode normalization and configured lowercasing for language-specific routes.
- Value: packed small binary blob of token ids + short checksum + serialized meta (lengths). Store as single allocation to reduce GC pressure.
- Size and eviction: per-host memory budget (configurable, default 64MB). Approx entry size estimate: 24 bytes overhead + 2 bytes/token. Use LRU with approximate frequency boost for same-tenant hits. TTL: 1h by default but configurable by route.
- Safety: cache is purely an optimization; if the tokenizer implementation changes, tokenizer_version bump invalidates. Cache must never change meaning of tokens; include tokenizer_version in keys.
- Multi-tenant isolation: track per-tenant quotas and separate eviction windows; tenant misbehavior cannot poison other tenants' entries.

Integration with KV cache for prefixes and serving runtime KV cache:
- Two-layer caching sense: (A) tokenization cache prevents repeated tokenization work, (B) prefix/KV caching at model token level remains for cached hidden states. Tokenization cache increases prefix cache hit rate indirectly (identical token sequences can use prefix cache).
- When tokenization cache hits, emit an event so scheduler can fast-path kernel selection and potentially reuse KV cache entries.

Scheduler interactions and kernel selection:
- Scheduler needs token-length distribution as early as possible. Tokenizer stage should provide token-length histogram for batch that helps select GPU kernel (e.g., prefer long-seq kernels vs short-seq).
- If a batch includes a mix of lengths, scheduler can shard into sub-batches by length class after tokenization. This is easier when tokenization is a separate stage.

Memory and performance engineering considerations:
- Avoid frequent allocations: reuse buffers for token arrays in tokenizer pools; use arena allocators for batch outputs.
- NUMA: pin tokenizer processes to CPU nodes nearest the NIC for low latency.
- Observability: emit per-request tokenization_time, tokenizer_hit (cache hit/miss), batch_size, batch_wait_time. Aggregate by route and tenant.

Metrics to collect (baseline + target):
- tokenization_latency_ms: p50/p95/p99 overall and by input-length bucket (<=16, 17–64, >64 tokens)
- tokenization_cache_hit_rate: global and per-route
- batch_size_distribution: avg and p99 when batching enabled
- end_to_end_latency_improvement: per-route delta pre/post
- memory_usage_token_cache: bytes used and evictions/sec

Experiment plan and microbenchmarks:
1) Microbench harness: replay production traces (sanitized) through a prototype tokenizer pool to measure latency and batch advantages. Measure both single-threaded and vectorized pipeline.
2) A/B rollout: start with a low-traffic route (internal dashboards) with tokenization cache disabled for other traffic. Monitor tokenization impact and memory.
3) Gradual increase: enable batching first without persistent cache, compare improvements; then enable local per-host cache; finally evaluate cross-host global cache only if hit-rate justifies network complexity.

Client-visible API and backward compatibility:
- No change to public Redwood API surface. Tokenization refactor is internal. However for customers using byte-level streaming, ensure streaming semantics unchanged.
- Consider offering an opt-in fast_tokenize RPC for advanced internal clients (console, eval harnesses) to pre-warm caches. This would be internal-only and rate-limited.

Risks and mitigations:
- Incorrect normalization/locale handling could lead to token id mismatches: require tokenizer_version and unit tests across locales.
- Memory growth from cache: guardrails (per-host caps, tenant caps, evict_rate alarms).
- Batching increases latency for some streaming patterns: provide per-route config to disable batching for streaming-enabled routes.

Open questions (to discuss):
- Is a per-host shared memory cache sufficient or do we need a small global distributed tokenization cache for very high duplicate rates? Cost/benefit unknown.
- How aggressive should TTLs be for multilingual workloads where normalization behavior varies?
- Should tokenizer pool be a separate process for crash isolation or an in-process thread pool? Crash isolation favors process boundary but has IPC cost.
- Can we reuse model tokenizer code across multiple languages without significant perf regressions?

Next steps and action items:
- Implement prototype tokenizer pool and batch API (owner: Marco Li) running in canary infra; target microbenchmarks by 2026-01-15.
- Add in-process LRU token cache prototype and dashboarding (owner: Aisha Gupta) by 2026-01-30.
- Produce end-to-end A/B test plan and rollback criteria (owner: Sofia Ramos) by 2026-02-10.
- Schedule architecture review with infra + serving runtime + product to align on per-route defaults and fail-open semantics.

Appendix: short example flows
1) Cache hit, batched: request arrives -> router assigns to tokenizer pool -> find cache key -> hit -> return token_ids quickly to scheduler -> scheduler selects kernel and KV prefix lookup likely successful -> reduced end-to-end latency.
2) Cache miss, batched: request batched with others -> tokenizer vectorized worker runs -> token_ids returned for batch -> scheduler shards by length and proceeds.
3) Streaming request: bypass batching and token cache; tokenize inline but on dedicated low-latency path to preserve streaming.

Notes to reviewers: please sanity-check the cache sizing numbers and eviction strategy. If you have production trace samples that show high identical short-input frequency, upload to the experiment harness link above. Specific implementation choices (in-process vs separate process) will heavily affect latency tradeoffs; we should prototype both minimal IPC and pure in-process pooling.
